title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, for every pair of finite one-relator presentations \[P=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_k\mid r=1\rangle,\qquad Q=\langle y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\mid s=1\rangle,\] where \(k,\ell\ge1\) and \(r,s\) are arbitrary explicitly written words in their respective generators and inverses, halts and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(G_P\cong G_Q\), and outputs \(0\) otherwise? Isomorphism is of abstract groups, with no condition on the images of the displayed generators. There is no running-time bound, promise on the presented groups, or restriction on the number of generators.
definitions:
For \(k\ge1\), a word is a finite sequence of letters \(x_i^{\epsilon}\), where \(1\le i\le k\) and \(\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}\). The empty word is allowed. The free group \(F_k\) consists of freely reduced words: adjacent inverse letters cancel, multiplication is concatenation followed by cancellation, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses a word and inverts each letter. The given relator need not be freely or cyclically reduced and may be a proper power. Its normal closure is
\[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle=\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{t} w_j r^{\epsilon_j}w_j^{-1}:t\ge0,\ w_j\in F_k,\ \epsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}\right\}.\]
Define \(G_P=F_k/\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle\), with two words \(u,v\) representing the same element exactly when \(uv^{-1}\) belongs to this normal closure; define \(G_Q\) in the same way. This specifies the meaning of a single relation \(r=1\) and the group operation on the quotient. A bijection \(\phi:G_P\to G_Q\) is a group isomorphism if \(\phi(gh)=\phi(g)\phi(h)\) for every \(g,h\in G_P\). It need not preserve a chosen generating tuple or lift to an automorphism of an ambient free group. The two presentations can have different numbers of generators, and all finite and infinite groups described by these presentations are included. The empty relator presents \(F_k\); the trivial group is included, for example by \(\langle x\mid x=1\rangle\).

Use the following concrete computable binary input encoding. For \(n\ge0\), let \(b\) be the length of the binary expansion of \(n+1\) with no leading zeroes, and encode \(n\) by \(u(n)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(n+1)\). If \(r\) has \(t\) letters, encode \(P\) by \(u(k)u(t)\) followed by, for each letter in order, one sign bit (\(0\) for \(+1\), \(1\) for \(-1\)) and \(u(i)\) for its generator index. Concatenate the encodings of \(P\) and \(Q\). Require \(k,\ell\ge1\), all indices in range, and no trailing bits. Thus validity is decidable from the finite string. Relators are explicit letter lists, with no compressed-word or binary-power notation in the input. A displayed power in mathematical examples denotes its fully expanded word in this encoding. Empty lists and unused generators are legal.

The machine has a finite description, ordinary read/write work tapes, and no oracle, advice or randomness. It must halt on every valid input pair and give the exact answer; it may be required to halt and output \(0\) on malformed strings without changing the question. There is no imposed time or space bound. One machine must handle all generator counts and relator lengths. No hyperbolicity certificate, torsion assumption, nontrivial-center promise or genericity assumption is supplied, and no explicit isomorphism witness need be printed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the specified isomorphism language is decidable or that it is undecidable. A positive answer supplies one finite algorithm and proves its termination and exact correctness for every valid pair in the stated encoding; all invoked decision subroutines require matching proved guarantees. A negative answer proves that every deterministic machine fails to halt with the correct bit on some valid pair, either through nontermination or an incorrect answer. A proved reduction from an undecidable problem qualifies only if it effectively produces pairs of the specified one-relator presentations and establishes both directions of the answer correspondence. Positive-instance semidecision, finite testing, a result for a proper subclass, or generic-case correctness is insufficient. A runtime lower bound alone is not undecidability. This is an exact yes/no question, without numerical tolerance.
why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.

importance.reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.

progress.text: Counterexamples to the Magnus conjecture separate abstract group isomorphism from free-group equivalence of relators; the 2025 survey describes the original examples and Brunner’s infinite family.
Pietrowski proves decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center; the survey records it as Corollary 1.7.3.
Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain establish generic rigidity for random one-relator groups.
Dahmani–Guirardel solve isomorphism for all hyperbolic groups; their Corollary 2 covers one-relator groups with torsion.
The survey retains the unrestricted torsion-free one-relator isomorphism problem as open.
A new preprint reports undecidability of the separate Diophantine problem in specified Baumslag–Gersten groups.
Kapovich’s preprint reports generic few-relator rigidity and restricted isomorphism algorithms with explicitly stated input hypotheses.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No uniform all-input isomorphism algorithm or undecidability theorem for arbitrary finite one-relator group presentations was found in the bounded primary-source review. The 2026 generic algorithms have explicit restrictions and fixed-parameter qualifications; the August Diophantine undecidability result concerns equations in fixed groups. Neither settles this unrestricted isomorphism question. New preprint proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: A finite presentation describes an abstract group, which may be infinite. Its displayed generators are names rather than a preferred basis intrinsic to the group. For example, \(\langle a,b\mid ba^{-2}=1\rangle\) and \(\langle x\mid\varepsilon=1\rangle\), with \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, both present the infinite cyclic group. The number of displayed generators and the spelling of the single relation therefore do not determine the isomorphism type.

Isomorphism is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality concerns two elements in one group, conjugacy concerns a particular relation between elements, and isomorphism compares the groups themselves. The single-relator restriction is strong enough for a uniform word algorithm, but the 2025 survey still records the general isomorphism question as unresolved.

An isomorphism between two finitely generated groups has a finite description by the images of the generators, and the inverse has such a description as well. This makes positive isomorphism instances semidecidable for finite presentations. Semidecidability provides no total decision procedure: the target also requires termination with a correct negative answer on every nonisomorphic pair.

Abelianization illustrates the difference between an invariant and a complete classification. The groups \(\langle a,b\mid\varepsilon=1\rangle\) and \(\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b^{-1}=1\rangle\) have the same abelianization \(\mathbb Z^2\), but the first is the nonabelian free group of rank two and the second is abelian. Thus even these elementary one-relator presentations agree on a natural algebraic invariant while representing different groups.

An automorphism of the ambient free group carrying one relator to the other, up to inversion, gives isomorphic quotient groups. Whitehead’s algorithm decides this free-group orbit problem. The converse fails: the Magnus conjecture was disproved, and Brunner exhibited a group with infinitely many pairwise inequivalent one-relator presentations. Abstract isomorphism is therefore a strictly broader comparison than that orbit test.

Dahmani and Guirardel give a uniform decision algorithm for isomorphism between presentations of hyperbolic groups, allowing torsion. Their Corollary 2 applies it to all one-relator groups with nontrivial torsion, because these groups are hyperbolic. This is a complete positive result for that subclass, not a resource-bound conjecture.

The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center. Nevertheless, arbitrary torsion-free one-relator groups are not covered by these results. The one-relator condition by itself does not imply hyperbolicity: the abelian group \(\mathbb Z^2\) already gives an example.

Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain prove strong isomorphism rigidity for an exponentially generic class of one-relator presentations with a fixed generator count. Here genericity refers to the proportion of long reduced relators in specified finite word models. A small exceptional set in that distribution can still contain inputs on which an all-input decision problem is unresolved.

Kapovich’s August 2026 preprint extends generic rigidity to fixed numbers of generators and relators. Theorem B describes polynomial-time recognizable generic classes with finite auxiliary data fixed separately for each parameter pair. Theorem C gives a quadratic-time algorithm comparing one fixed generic presentation with suitable small-cancellation presentations, and a linear-time comparison when both inputs are promised to belong to the stated generic classes. These hypotheses exclude arbitrary one-relator input pairs; the generic-family result does not supply the uniform total algorithm asked for here.

Nyberg-Brodda’s August 2026 preprint reports undecidability of solving systems of equations with coefficients in specified one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. Its input consists of equations inside a fixed group, whereas this card compares two group presentations. The theorem does not by itself provide an undecidability reduction for the isomorphism problem.

A positive resolution would establish effective classification of all groups in this concise presentation format, even if the algorithm were extremely slow. A negative resolution would show that abstract group type remains undecidable within a class whose word problem is decidable. Both outcomes concern a computability boundary rather than the practical speed of existing group software.

category_assignment.reason: The main task recognizes isomorphism of group presentations, not term unification.

sentences: A finite one-relator presentation describes a group using finitely many generators and one explicitly written relation.
The question asks for one algorithm deciding whether any two such presentations define isomorphic abstract groups, even with different generator counts.
The answer must be exact and the algorithm must always terminate, but there is no running-time bound or geometric promise.
A complete Lean proof must establish this uniform decision procedure or prove undecidability for the exact input class.
Known hyperbolic and center subclasses, generic rigidity algorithms and the 2026 undecidability result for equations in fixed groups do not resolve the all-input comparison.

source_formulation.text: Retains the unrestricted one-relator presentation-isomorphism question recorded in the survey, with arbitrary finite generator counts and abstract group isomorphisms. The empty-relator convention and concrete finite encoding make inputs explicit; they do not impose torsion, geometric or generic promises. No complexity bound is added.
